periods.activity_title: What Floor Are You On? Meeting Negative Numbers

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Activity 1, p.243
textbook_items_in_class.description: Students identify floors and their numbers in Bela's Building of Fun from a diagram, and determine what to press on the lift to travel four floors up and three floors down.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.1 p.245
textbook_items_in_class.description: Start from Floor +2 and press –3. Where do you reach? Write an expression.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Addition to keep track of movement), p.245
textbook_items_in_class.description: Starting from Food Court (Floor +1), pressing +2 in the lift leads to target floor (+1)+(+2)=+3, illustrating the rule Starting Floor + Movement = Target Floor.

time_bands.activity: Introduce Bela's Building of Fun using Activity 1, p.243 ("Students identify floors and their numbers in Bela's Building of Fun...."). Draw the building on the board — Ground Floor as 0, floors above as positive, floors below as negative. Ask students to name the floor of the Toy Store, Cinema, Food Court, and Ice Cream shop, reading labels from the diagram.

Walk through Example (Addition to keep track of movement), p.245 ("Starting from Food Court (Floor +1), pressing +2...."). Introduce the rule Starting Floor + Movement = Target Floor. Students copy the building sketch and annotate each floor's number, then predict: 'If you are on Floor –2 and press +4, where do you arrive?' — confirming by counting up the diagram.

Students attempt Figure it Out Q1, section 10.1 p.245 ("Start from Floor +2 and press –3. Where do you reach?...."). Pairs share answers aloud and write the corresponding addition expression. Draw attention to the sign of the result and ask: 'What does a negative floor number mean in the building?'

Class discussion: invite students to state, in their own words, what a positive floor number and a negative floor number each mean. Record two or three student formulations on the board as a reference definition for the integer naming convention established in this unit.

periods.teacher_notes: The Building of Fun diagram is the primary scaffold — spend time ensuring every student can match a floor name to its integer label before moving to expressions. A common early error is writing the movement without a sign (writing 3 instead of +3 or –3); prompt students to always include the direction sign. Example (Addition to keep track of movement), p.245 is the anchor worked example for the rule; students who want a second reading may revisit it independently.

periods.activity_title: Combining Button Presses and the Back-to-Zero Idea

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Combining button presses), p.245
textbook_items_in_class.description: Gurmit presses +2 by mistake then –3 to correct; result is (+2)+(–3)=–1, illustrating that combining button presses is addition.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Back to zero), p.246
textbook_items_in_class.description: Pressing +3 and then –3 returns to Floor 0; introduces the concept of additive inverse. (+3)+(–3)=0.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 10.1 p.246
textbook_items_in_class.description: Evaluate four expressions (a–d) as combined button presses: (+1)+(+4), (+4)+(+1), (+4)+(–3)+(–2), (–1)+(+2)+(–3).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.1 p.245
textbook_items_in_class.description: Evaluate seven expressions (a–g) as Starting Floor + Movement: (+1)+(+4), (+4)+(+1), (+4)+(–3), (–1)+(+2), (–1)+(+1), 0+(+2), 0+(–2).

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 10.1 p.245
homework.description: Find multiple starting floors and the movements needed to reach Floor –5; write expressions of the form (starting)+(movement)=–5.

time_bands.activity: Pose the scenario: 'You press +2 in the lift by mistake, then press –3 to try to fix it. What floor do you end up on?' Allow students to guess, then examine Example (Combining button presses), p.245 ("Gurmit presses +2 by mistake then –3 to correct; result (+2)+(–3)=–1...."). Establish that the sequence of presses is itself an addition.

Introduce Example (Back to zero), p.246 ("Pressing +3 and then –3 returns to Floor 0; introduces additive inverse...."). Ask: 'What single press would undo +5? What about –7?' Students discover the additive inverse pattern and record their findings.

Students work on Figure it Out Q2, section 10.1 p.245 ("Evaluate seven expressions (a–g) as Starting Floor + Movement....") and Figure it Out, section 10.1 p.246 ("Evaluate four expressions (a–d) as combined button presses...."). Encourage small-group discussion and comparison of methods for the three-press expressions.

Gallery-style share: ask two or three pairs to explain how they evaluated a multi-press expression. Record the 'Back to Zero' finding — that pressing +n and then –n always returns to the starting floor — as a class conjecture on the board.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established that floor numbers are signed integers, this unit deepens the structure by showing that a sequence of presses is just a sum. Watch for students who add the absolute values regardless of sign; the building diagram is the best corrective — trace each press step by step on the sketch. Example (Back to zero), p.246 is the gateway to additive inverse; make sure students articulate why the result is 0 in their own words before moving on.

periods.activity_title: Ordering Integers: Which Floor Is Lower?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.1 p.247
textbook_items_in_class.description: Compare six pairs of integers using < or > by referring to the Building of Fun: –2 vs +5, –5 vs +4, –5 vs –3, +6 vs –6, 0 vs –4, 0 vs +4.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.1 p.247
textbook_items_in_class.description: Compare six pairs of larger integers with < or >: –10 vs –12, +17 vs –10, 0 vs –20, +9 vs –9, –25 vs –7, +15 vs –17.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 10.1 p.247
textbook_items_in_class.description: Given Floor A=–12, Floor D=–1, Floor E=+1 on a vertical number line, find the numbers of Floors B, C, F, G, and H.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 10.1 p.247
textbook_items_in_class.description: Mark four floors (–7, –4, +3, –10) on a vertical building diagram.

time_bands.activity: Draw a tall vertical number line on the board (–5 to +5). Ask: 'Floor –4 and Floor –3 — which is lower in the building?' Invite students to point on the diagram. Establish the comparison rule: lower on the building means a smaller number, formalising the < relation for negative integers.

Students complete Figure it Out Q1, section 10.1 p.247 ("Compare six pairs of integers using < or > by referring to the Building of Fun....") and Figure it Out Q2, section 10.1 p.247 ("Compare six pairs of larger integers with < or >...."). Ask students to explain each answer using the building image — not just the symbol.

Students work on Figure it Out Q3, section 10.1 p.247 ("Given Floor A=–12, Floor D=–1, Floor E=+1 on a vertical number line, find Floors B, C, F, G, H....") and Figure it Out Q4, section 10.1 p.247 ("Mark four floors (–7, –4, +3, –10) on a vertical building diagram...."). Discuss Q3 as a class, focusing on equal spacing between floors.

Quick-fire oral round: teacher says a pair of integers, students hold up a thumb-up for the first being greater or thumb-down for the first being smaller. Consolidate with the key observation: among negative integers, the one with the larger absolute value is always the smaller integer.

periods.teacher_notes: Having built intuition for negative floors through addition, this unit formalises ordering. The most persistent error is thinking –5 > –3 because 5 > 3; anchoring comparison to the building diagram — 'which floor is physically lower?' — reliably corrects this. Figure it Out Q3, section 10.1 p.247 is particularly useful for extending ordering to unlabelled positions on a number line; work through one item together before releasing students.

periods.activity_title: Subtraction as Finding the Movement Needed

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Subtraction a), p.249
textbook_items_in_class.description: Target Floor –1, Starting Floor –2: movement needed is (+1). Expression: (–1)–(–2)=(+1).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Subtraction b), p.249
textbook_items_in_class.description: Target Floor –1, Starting Floor +3: movement needed is –4. Expression: (–1)–(+3)=(–4).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Subtraction c), p.249
textbook_items_in_class.description: Target Floor +2, Starting Floor –2: movement needed is +4. Expression: (+2)–(–2)=(+4).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 10.1 p.249
textbook_items_in_class.description: Complete ten subtraction expressions (a–j) as movement from Starting Floor to Target Floor: (+1)–(+4), 0–(+2), (+4)–(+1), 0–(–2), (+4)–(–3), (–4)–(–3), (–1)–(+2), (–2)–(–2), (–1)–(+1), (+3)–(–3).

time_bands.activity: Pose: 'You want to go from Floor –2 to Floor –1. What do you press?' Frame the question as Target Floor – Starting Floor = Movement. Examine Example (Subtraction a), p.249 ("Target Floor –1, Starting Floor –2: movement needed is (+1)....") and Example (Subtraction b), p.249 ("Target Floor –1, Starting Floor +3: movement needed is –4....").

Work through Example (Subtraction c), p.249 ("Target Floor +2, Starting Floor –2: movement needed is +4...."). Ask students to verify the result by starting at –2 and pressing +4 on the building diagram, arriving at +2. Draw attention to the case of subtracting a negative: the movement is larger than expected, and in the positive direction.

Students independently complete Figure it Out, section 10.1 p.249 ("Complete ten subtraction expressions (a–j) as movement from Starting Floor to Target Floor...."). After completing each expression, students check their answers by reversing: starting floor + movement = target floor.

Class debrief on items (d) 0–(–2) and (e) (+4)–(–3), which require subtracting a negative. Record the emerging pattern — subtracting a negative gives a larger positive movement — on the board as a conjecture to be revisited.

periods.teacher_notes: Having established addition of integers through the lift, subtraction is now reframed as 'how far and in which direction do you need to press?' This frame resolves most computational errors. Watch for students writing the movement without considering direction when crossing zero; the verification step (start + movement = target) is the key self-check. Example (Subtraction c), p.249 is the critical worked example for subtracting a negative; do not rush past it.

periods.activity_title: Larger Integers: Mine Shafts and the Infinite Lift

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Adding larger numbers, mine), p.250
Example (Infinite lift subtraction), p.251
textbook_items_in_class.description: Computing +2000–(–200): going from –200 to +2000 on the infinite lift requires pressing +2200. Reveals that subtracting a negative equals adding a positive.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 10.1 p.251
textbook_items_in_class.description: Complete seven expressions using the mine/larger number context (a–g): (+40)+__=+200, (+40)+__=–200, (–50)+__=+200, (–50)+__=–200, (–200)–(–40), (+200)–(+40), (–200)–(+40). Verify using the mineshaft.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 10.1 p.251

time_bands.activity: Introduce the mine context from Example (Adding larger numbers, mine), p.250 ("Mine context: (+40)+(+60)=+100 and (–90)+(–55)=–145 for addition; (+40)–(–50)=+90 and (–90)–(+40)=–130...."). Stress that the same Starting Floor + Movement rule applies regardless of the size of the numbers.

Examine Example (Infinite lift subtraction), p.251 ("Computing +2000–(–200): going from –200 to +2000 requires pressing +2200...."). Ask: 'Is pressing +2200 the same as adding +2200? And is going from –200 to +2000 the same as +2000+(+200)?' Draw the key equivalence: subtracting a negative equals adding the corresponding positive.

Students work through Figure it Out, section 10.1 p.251 (both sets: "Complete seven expressions using the mine/larger number context...." and "Evaluate eight expressions by imagining a suitable lift...."). Students who finish early are asked to verify their answers by converting each subtraction of a negative into addition.

Consolidation: students write one sentence in their own words explaining why subtracting a negative number gives the same result as adding its positive counterpart. Two or three sentences are shared and discussed.

periods.teacher_notes: Having shown subtraction of integers with small numbers, this unit extends the model to three- and four-digit integers, where mental tracking of the building is harder. The mine context anchors larger numbers concretely; do not skip it in favour of symbolic rules. Students often struggle with expressions like –99+(+200) because they expect a negative result; the number-line image of moving right from –99 by 200 steps is the clarifying picture. Example (Infinite lift subtraction), p.251 is a self-study reference for students who want a second walk-through of the equivalence.

periods.activity_title: The Number Line and Converting Subtraction to Addition

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.1 p.253
textbook_items_in_class.description: Mark 3 positive and 3 negative numbers on a given number line (–10 to +10).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 10.1 p.254
textbook_items_in_class.description: Is 2 > –3? Why? Is –2 < 3? Why? Justify using the number line.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Unmarked number line addition), p.254
textbook_items_in_class.description: UNL showing 85+(–60)=25 by marking –60 movement from +85.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Unmarked number line subtraction), p.254
textbook_items_in_class.description: UNL showing (–100)–(+250)=–350 by interpreting subtraction as missing addend.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Conversion subtraction to addition), p.255
textbook_items_in_class.description: Breaking journey from 2 to –3: (a) 2→0 is –2, (b) 0→–3 is –3; total movement is –3+(–2)=–5. Shows –3–2=–5 with no subtraction in second form.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out, section 10.1 p.255
textbook_items_in_class.description: Use unmarked number lines to evaluate four expressions: –125+(–30), +105–(–55), +80–(–150), –99–(–200).

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 10.1 p.254

time_bands.activity: Draw a horizontal integer number line (–10 to +10) on the board. Students complete Figure it Out Q1, section 10.1 p.253 ("Mark 3 positive and 3 negative numbers on a given number line....") and Figure it Out Q3, section 10.1 p.254 ("Is 2 > –3? Why? Is –2 < 3? Why? Justify using the number line...."). Reinforce: rightward on the number line means greater.

Walk through Example (Unmarked number line addition), p.254 ("UNL showing 85+(–60)=25 by marking –60 movement from +85....") and Example (Unmarked number line subtraction), p.254 ("UNL showing (–100)–(+250)=–350 by interpreting subtraction as missing addend...."). Show how to draw a quick sketch line with only the relevant numbers labelled.

Introduce Example (Conversion subtraction to addition), p.255 ("Breaking journey from 2 to –3: 2→0 is –2, 0→–3 is –3; total –3+(–2)=–5...."). Students then attempt Figure it Out, section 10.1 p.255 ("Use unmarked number lines to evaluate four expressions: –125+(–30), +105–(–55), +80–(–150), –99–(–200)...."), drawing their own sketched number lines.

Pair-share: each student explains to their partner how they drew the number line for one of their expressions. Class agrees on the conversion rule — subtracting a positive is moving left; subtracting a negative is moving right — and students record the rule in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: Having worked with the building and mine contexts, this unit moves integer arithmetic onto the horizontal number line and introduces the unmarked number line as a flexible computation tool. Students sometimes draw their number lines too short, cutting off the endpoint; insist they label at least the start and the end of their arrow. Example (Conversion subtraction to addition), p.255 unifies the entire arc of section 10.1; treat it as a culminating moment and allow extra time for the pair-share discussion.

periods.activity_title: Tokens in Your Pocket: Adding Integers Concretely

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Token addition +5 and –8), p.256
textbook_items_in_class.description: Lay out 5 positive and 8 negative tokens; remove 5 zero pairs; 3 negative tokens remain. (+5)+(–8)=–3.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.2 p.257
textbook_items_in_class.description: Complete four additions using token diagrams: (+6)+(+4), (–3)+(–2), (+5)+(–7), (–2)+(+6).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.2 p.257
textbook_items_in_class.description: Cancel zero pairs in two given token sets (a: 3 positive + 5 negative; b: 6 positive + 3 negative). State which floor the attendant is on and write the corresponding addition statement.

time_bands.activity: Students make quick paper tokens: tear a sheet into small squares, mark half '+' (positive) and half '–' (negative). Introduce the zero-pair rule: one '+' token and one '–' token together make 0 and can be removed. Demonstrate with three positive and three negative tokens on a desk.

Work through Example (Token addition +5 and –8), p.256 ("Lay out 5 positive and 8 negative tokens; remove 5 zero pairs; 3 negative tokens remain. (+5)+(–8)=–3....") using physical tokens on the board ledge. Students replicate the layout at their desks.

Students complete Figure it Out Q1, section 10.2 p.257 ("Complete four additions using token diagrams: (+6)+(+4), (–3)+(–2), (+5)+(–7), (–2)+(+6)....") and Figure it Out Q2, section 10.2 p.257 ("Cancel zero pairs in two given token sets....") using their paper tokens. Pairs check each other's results.

Discussion: 'Does it matter which zero pairs you remove first, or does the order matter?' Students argue from their token experience and arrive at the conclusion that the final count is independent of which pairs are removed. Record this observation.

periods.teacher_notes: The token model provides a manipulative anchor that explains integer addition without relying on rules to memorise. Watch for students who forget to remove all zero pairs — they will report a larger absolute value than is correct. The floor metaphor (the attendant's pocket) connects the token model back to the Building of Fun framework built in section 10.1; name that connection explicitly.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Token subtraction +5 minus +4), p.257
textbook_items_in_class.description: From 5 positives, remove 4; 1 positive remains. (+5)–(+4)=+1.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Token subtraction –7 minus –5), p.257
textbook_items_in_class.description: From 7 negatives, remove 5; 2 negatives remain. (–7)–(–5)=–2. Also prompts: is this the same as (–7)+(+5)?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Token subtraction +5 minus +6), p.257-258
textbook_items_in_class.description: 5 positives, need to remove 6 — not enough. Add one zero pair; now remove 6 positives; 1 negative left. (+5)–(+6)=–1.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Example (Token subtraction +4 minus –6), p.258
textbook_items_in_class.description: 4 positives, need to remove 6 negatives — none present. Add 6 zero pairs (6 positives + 6 negatives); remove 6 negatives; 10 positives remain. +4–(–6)=+10.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.2 p.258
Figure it Out Q1, section 10.2 p.259
textbook_items_in_class.description: Subtract –3–(+5) using tokens. How many zero pairs are needed? What is the result?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.2 p.259

time_bands.activity: Walk through Example (Token subtraction +5 minus +4), p.257 ("From 5 positives, remove 4; 1 positive remains....") and Example (Token subtraction –7 minus –5), p.257 ("From 7 negatives, remove 5; 2 negatives remain...."). Students use paper tokens at their desks to replicate both. Pose the link question from WE-14: 'Is (–7)–(–5) the same as (–7)+(+5)?'

Introduce the challenge: 'You have 5 positive tokens but need to remove 6.' Examine Example (Token subtraction +5 minus +6), p.257-258 ("5 positives, not enough — add one zero pair; remove 6; 1 negative left....") and Example (Token subtraction +4 minus –6), p.258 ("4 positives, need to remove 6 negatives — add 6 zero pairs...."). Students act both out with their tokens.

Students complete Figure it Out Q1, section 10.2 p.258 ("Evaluate six differences using tokens: (+10)–(+7), (–8)–(–4)....") and Figure it Out Q1, section 10.2 p.259 ("Subtract –3–(+5) using tokens. How many zero pairs are needed?...."). Students record both the token diagram and the numeric expression for each.

Students articulate in one sentence the key insight: 'When you subtract a negative, you add zero pairs and remove the negatives, leaving extra positives — so subtracting a negative is the same as adding a positive.' Share two responses.

periods.teacher_notes: Having mastered token addition in the previous unit, students now extend tokens to subtraction, including the critical zero-pair borrowing technique. The hardest case is subtracting a negative when none of that type is present; walk slowly through Example (Token subtraction +4 minus –6), p.258 and confirm the result against the building/number-line answer of +10. Watch for students adding only one zero pair when they need several; stress that the number of zero pairs added must equal the number of tokens being removed.

periods.activity_title: Bank Balances and Below-Sea Heights: Real Integers

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.3 p.260
textbook_items_in_class.description: Bank account: start at ₹0, add credits of ₹30, ₹40, ₹50 and debits of ₹40, ₹50, ₹60. What is the balance?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.3 p.260
textbook_items_in_class.description: Bank account: start at ₹0, debits of ₹1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 and a single credit of ₹256. What is the balance?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 10.3 p.260
textbook_items_in_class.description: Why is it generally better to keep a positive bank balance? When might a temporary negative balance be worthwhile?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.3 p.261
textbook_items_in_class.description: Read heights A–G from a geographical cross-section chart and fill in the values.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.3 p.261
textbook_items_in_class.description: Identify the highest and lowest points in the geographical cross-section.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 10.3 p.261
textbook_items_in_class.description: Write points A–G in decreasing and increasing order of heights.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the banking context: credits are positive changes to a balance, debits are negative changes. Pose: 'If your account has ₹0 and you deposit ₹100 then spend ₹130, what happens?' Establish that a negative balance is a meaningful and real integer.

Students work through Figure it Out Q1, section 10.3 p.260 ("Bank account: start at ₹0, credits ₹30, ₹40, ₹50 and debits ₹40, ₹50, ₹60...."), Figure it Out Q2, section 10.3 p.260 ("Start at ₹0, debits of ₹1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128 and credit ₹256...."), and Figure it Out Q3, section 10.3 p.260 ("Why is it generally better to keep a positive bank balance?...."). Q3 is discussed briefly as a class.

Transition to geographical heights. Students read Figure it Out Q1, section 10.3 p.261 ("Read heights A–G from a geographical cross-section chart...."), Figure it Out Q2, section 10.3 p.261 ("Identify highest and lowest points...."), and Figure it Out Q3, section 10.3 p.261 ("Write points A–G in decreasing and increasing order....") using the cross-section diagram in the textbook.
Class comparison: 'Which real-world context — banking or geography — makes negative numbers feel most natural to you and why?' Brief show-of-hands poll followed by two student explanations.

periods.teacher_notes: Having practised integer arithmetic symbolically, this unit grounds the operations in two everyday contexts where integers arise naturally. Students are sometimes confused by Figure it Out Q2, section 10.3 p.260 because the debits double each time — encourage them to list the debits and sum them before computing the final balance. For the geography questions, ensure students can locate sea level as zero on the cross-section chart before reading heights.

periods.activity_title: Sub-Zero Temperatures: Integers in Climate Data

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 10.3 p.261
textbook_items_in_class.description: What is the highest point above sea level on Earth and its height?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 10.3 p.261
textbook_items_in_class.description: What is the lowest point on Earth with respect to sea level? What is its (negative) height?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.3 p.262
textbook_items_in_class.description: Research and find places in India where temperatures go below 0°C. What do they have in common and why?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.3 p.262
textbook_items_in_class.description: Match four temperatures (14°C, 8°C, –2°C, –4°C) with four times of day in Leh, Ladakh in November.

time_bands.activity: Begin with the Earth extremes: students answer Figure it Out Q4, section 10.3 p.261 ("What is the highest point above sea level on Earth?....") and Figure it Out Q5, section 10.3 p.261 ("What is the lowest point on Earth with respect to sea level?....") using the textbook or recalled knowledge. Record the heights as signed integers and place them on a quick number line sketch.

Introduce temperature: 0°C is the freezing point of water; temperatures below are negative. Students discuss Figure it Out Q1, section 10.3 p.262 ("Research and find places in India where temperatures go below 0°C. What do they have in common?....") in small groups, drawing on knowledge of high-altitude and desert regions.

Students complete Figure it Out Q2, section 10.3 p.262 ("Match four temperatures (14°C, 8°C, –2°C, –4°C) with four times of day in Leh, Ladakh in November...."). Ask them to order the temperatures on a number line, then justify their matching using both integer ordering and knowledge of how temperatures change through the day.

Wrap-up: students write one integer expression that captures a temperature change (e.g., from –4°C at 4 a.m. to +8°C at 2 p.m. is a change of +12°C) and share with the class. Reinforce that integer subtraction quantifies change in any signed context.

periods.teacher_notes: Having used integers in banking and geography, this unit adds the temperature context, completing the three real-world strands of section 10.3. Students who say sub-zero temperatures are impossible should be asked to name mountain or polar locations — their intuitions about altitude are a useful bridge. The matching exercise (Figure it Out Q2, section 10.3 p.262) rewards both integer ordering and contextual reasoning, so encourage students to explain their match rather than guess.

periods.activity_title: Hollow Integer Grids: Filling Borders to a Target Sum

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.4 p.263
textbook_items_in_class.description: Compute the four border sums (top row, bottom row, left column, right column) for the second hollow integer grid and identify the border sum.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.4 p.264
textbook_items_in_class.description: Complete three hollow integer grids to achieve specified border sums: +4, –2, –4.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 10.4 p.264
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find more than one way to fill the border-sum –4 grid.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 10.4 p.264
textbook_items_in_class.description: Which grids can be filled in multiple ways? What could be the reason?

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 10.4 p.264
homework.description: Make a border integer square puzzle and challenge classmates.

time_bands.activity: Draw a 3×3 hollow grid on the board (only border cells visible, centre empty). Explain the rule: the top row, bottom row, left column, and right column must all sum to the same 'border sum'. Demonstrate checking sums on the first example grid in the textbook.

Students complete Figure it Out Q1, section 10.4 p.263 ("Compute the four border sums for the second hollow integer grid and identify the border sum...."). After checking the sums, ask: 'Can you predict the border sum before computing it, just by looking at the numbers?'

Students attempt Figure it Out Q2, section 10.4 p.264 ("Complete three hollow integer grids: border sums +4, –2, –4....") and Figure it Out Q3, section 10.4 p.264 ("Find more than one way to fill the border-sum –4 grid...."). Pairs compare their different fillings for the –4 grid and verify both.

Class discussion on Figure it Out Q4, section 10.4 p.264 ("Which grids can be filled in multiple ways? What could be the reason?...."). Students reason about what property of the border sum or available numbers allows multiple solutions, building a conjecture together.

periods.teacher_notes: This unit marks the transition from applying known procedures to reasoning about structure — students must think about why multiple fillings are or are not possible, not just compute a single answer. A common error is computing row and column sums independently without checking that the corner cells are shared between a row and a column; draw attention to the corners explicitly. Figure it Out Q3, section 10.4 p.264 is the key reasoning task: push students to explain why two different fillings both work, not just to exhibit them.

periods.activity_title: The Amazing Grid: Discovering an Invariant Sum

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.4 p.265
textbook_items_in_class.description: In the amazing grid, try the circle-and-strike game afresh with different chosen numbers. Does the final sum change?

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.4 p.265
textbook_items_in_class.description: Play the circle-and-strike game on two other provided 4×4 grids (arithmetic progression grids).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 10.4 p.265
textbook_items_in_class.description: What is special about these grids — is the 'magic' in the numbers, the arrangement, or both? Can you make more such grids?

time_bands.activity: Demonstrate the circle-and-strike game on the board with the 4×4 amazing grid: circle one number, strike its row and column, circle another unstruck number, strike its row and column, and repeat until four numbers are circled. Add the four circled numbers. Ask students to predict what happens if the first choice is different.

Students independently try Figure it Out Q1, section 10.4 p.265 ("Try the circle-and-strike game afresh with different chosen numbers. Does the final sum change?....") with at least three different starting choices. They record each set of four circled numbers and their sums.

Students play Figure it Out Q2, section 10.4 p.265 ("Play the circle-and-strike game on two other provided 4×4 grids....") and then tackle Figure it Out Q3, section 10.4 p.265 ("What is special about these grids — is the magic in the numbers, the arrangement, or both? Can you make more such grids?....") in pairs, trying to construct their own grid that has the same invariant property.

Whole-class reasoning: 'Is the invariant sum caused by the specific numbers chosen, the way the grid is arranged, or both?' Invite two or three explanatory conjectures and record them on the board without adjudicating — the investigation continues as open inquiry.

periods.teacher_notes: The amazing grid's invariance is the key discovery of this unit; resist giving the algebraic explanation immediately and allow students to conjecture first — the experience of noticing the pattern inductively is the mathematical goal. Watch for students who verify only two trials and assume the pattern holds; push for a third and fourth to build genuine conviction. Figure it Out Q3, section 10.4 p.265 is the richest reasoning challenge — asking students to build their own grid brings structural understanding without algebraic formalism.

periods.activity_title: Integer Consolidation: Sequences, Cards, and Sign Reasoning

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 10.4 p.265
textbook_items_in_class.description: Solve eight integer arithmetic expressions arranged in a 2×4 table: 8–13, (–8)–(13), (–13)–(–8), (–13)+(–8), 8+(–13), (–8)–(–13), (13)–8, 13–(–8).

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q6, section 10.4 p.266
Figure it Out Q7, section 10.4 p.266
textbook_items_in_class.description: From six integer cards (+1, +7, +18, –5, –2, –9), construct an addition/subtraction expression whose value is closest to –30.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q8, section 10.4 p.266
textbook_items_in_class.description: Determine whether each of six types of integer addition/subtraction combinations [(positive)–(negative), (positive)+(negative), (negative)+(negative), (negative)–(negative), (negative)–(positive), (negative)+(positive)] is always positive, always negative, or can be either.

homework.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.4 p.265
homework.description: Write all integers between four given pairs in increasing order: (a) 0 and –7, (b) –4 and 4, (c) –8 and –15, (d) –30 and –23.

time_bands.activity: Students complete Figure it Out Q4, section 10.4 p.265 ("Solve eight integer arithmetic expressions in a 2×4 table: 8–13, (–8)–(13), (–13)–(–8)...."). Ask: 'Which pairs of expressions give the same answer? Why?' This launches reasoning about how changing the sign of a term affects the result.

Students work on Figure it Out Q6, section 10.4 p.266 ("Complete three integer sequences: (a) (–40),(–34),(–28),(–22),....; (b) 3,4,2,5,....; (c) __,__,12,6,1,(–3),(–6),....) identifying the rule and reasoning about pattern, then Figure it Out Q7, section 10.4 p.266 ("From six integer cards (+1,+7,+18,–5,–2,–9), construct an expression closest to –30....") as a creative challenge.

Students tackle Figure it Out Q8, section 10.4 p.266 ("Determine whether each of six types of integer combinations is always positive, always negative, or can be either....") in pairs, generating examples and counterexamples. The goal is to reason from examples to a general claim, not to memorise a rule.

Class shares conclusions for Figure it Out Q8, section 10.4 p.266 — particularly the cases that 'can be either'. Students articulate: 'Which types can we determine the sign of without computing, and which cannot?' Record the agreed answers.

periods.teacher_notes: Having explored grid puzzles, this unit consolidates integer arithmetic through reasoning tasks — sign analysis, sequence completion, and strategic card use — rather than routine computation. Figure it Out Q8, section 10.4 p.266 is the richest reasoning item; students who say '(positive)+(negative) is always negative' should be asked to try +10+(–3) as a counterexample, building their habit of testing claims with examples. The sequence in part (b) of Figure it Out Q6 is non-obvious — its alternating interleaved structure may require a hint to notice.

periods.activity_title: History Through Integers and the Token String Puzzle

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.4 p.265
textbook_items_in_class.description: Give three integers whose sum is –8.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q3, section 10.4 p.265
textbook_items_in_class.description: Two dice with faces –1, 2, –3, 4, –5, 6. Find the numbers between –10 and +12 that cannot be obtained as a sum of the two dice.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q5, section 10.4 p.265-266
textbook_items_in_class.description: Find three historical years: (a) 150 years before the present year, (b) 2200 years before the present year (no year 0), (c) 320 years after 680 BCE.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q9, section 10.4 p.266
textbook_items_in_class.description: A string of 100 tokens in a repeating pattern (+++––). What is the total value of the string?

time_bands.activity: Students explore Figure it Out Q2, section 10.4 p.265 ("Give three integers whose sum is –8....") — invite multiple answers from the class and ask if there are infinitely many such triples. Then tackle Figure it Out Q3, section 10.4 p.265 ("Two dice with faces –1, 2, –3, 4, –5, 6. Find numbers between –10 and +12 that cannot be obtained as a sum....") — pairs list all achievable sums by pairing faces.

Examine Figure it Out Q5, section 10.4 p.265-266 ("Find three historical years: (a) 150 years before present, (b) 2200 years before present with no year 0, (c) 320 years after 680 BCE...."). Discuss what 'no year 0' means on the integer timeline, and how to adjust the calculation for part (b).

Students work through Figure it Out Q9, section 10.4 p.266 ("A string of 100 tokens in repeating pattern +++––. What is the total value?...."). Guide students to identify the repeating unit (+++–– = 3 positives + 2 negatives = net +1 per 5 tokens), determine how many complete units fit in 100, and compute the total.

Discussion: 'What reasoning strategy did you use to avoid adding 100 individual tokens?' Students name the strategy — finding a repeating unit and scaling — and connect it to earlier ideas about additive inverse (zero pairs cancel within a pattern).

periods.teacher_notes: This unit brings together several strands of integer reasoning — open-ended sum-finding, enumeration of dice outcomes, historical timeline computation, and pattern-based reasoning — giving students practice in choosing an appropriate approach for each problem type. The historical years question (Figure it Out Q5, section 10.4 p.265-266) often surprises students with the no-year-zero adjustment; acknowledge this as a genuine mathematical quirk of the BCE/CE calendar, not an error. The token-string puzzle rewards systematic thinking over brute-force counting — reward explanations of method, not just correct answers.

periods.activity_title: Brahmagupta's Rules: Ancient Arithmetic Meets the Number Line

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.5 p.268
textbook_items_in_class.description: Explain each of Brahmagupta's rules for addition and subtraction in terms of Bela's Building of Fun or the number line.

textbook_items_in_class.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.5 p.268
textbook_items_in_class.description: Give your own examples of each of Brahmagupta's rules for addition and subtraction.

time_bands.activity: Introduce the history: Brahmagupta's Brāhma-sphuṭa-siddhānta (628 CE) gave the first complete explicit rules for adding and subtracting positive numbers, negative numbers, and zero. Read two or three of his five addition rules aloud from the textbook (section 10.5). Ask students: 'Which rule matches the additive inverse we found in the building?'

Students work on Figure it Out Q1, section 10.5 p.268 ("Explain each of Brahmagupta's rules for addition and subtraction in terms of Bela's Building of Fun or the number line...."). For each rule, students write one sentence connecting the abstract rule to a concrete lift scenario, working individually then comparing with a partner.

Students complete Figure it Out Q2, section 10.5 p.268 ("Give your own examples of each of Brahmagupta's rules for addition and subtraction...."). Each student invents a numerical example for at least three rules and verifies the answer using the number line or conversion method.

Brief discussion: 'Brahmagupta wrote these rules 1400 years ago. Are they the same as the rules we have been using throughout this chapter?' Students confirm the equivalence and note that the chapter's discovery-based approach re-derived rules that took centuries to formalise historically.

periods.teacher_notes: Brahmagupta's rules are the formal culmination of the chapter's arithmetic arc; this unit asks students to read historical mathematical text and translate it into familiar language, a genuinely different cognitive demand. Students sometimes struggle with rules stated in terms of 'fortunes' (positive) and 'debts' (negative) — draw the parallel to the building's above-ground and below-ground floors immediately. Figure it Out Q1, section 10.5 p.268 is the primary task; ensure students explain every rule, not just the ones they find easy.

periods.activity_title: Integers at Work: Four Problems, Four Methods
periods.teacher_notes: Pose all four problems at once on the board. Students work individually for 15 minutes with full written working, then compare answers in groups of three for 8 minutes — any disagreement must be reconstructed step by step, not just announced. Each group then nominates one presenter per problem; after each presentation the class names the chapter method used. Watch for: Problem 1 — students must apply the additive-inverse idea, not just guess; warn against writing the answer without showing the cancellation. Problem 2 — the subtraction-as-movement method (target minus start); the most common error is reversing the direction, giving +145 instead of −145. Problem 3 — token subtraction requiring zero pairs; students who skip the zero-pair step and just 'know the rule' should be asked to draw the tokens. Problem 4 — integer comparison and ordering; watch for students who place negative numbers in the wrong order relative to each other.

visual_aids.title: Problems and solutions
visual_aids.table:
No. | Problem | Solution
1 | Riya is on Floor +5 in a building. She presses −8 in the lift, then presses +3. What floor does she end on? Show that her two presses together have a combined effect. | Start: +5. Combined button press: (−8)+(+3) = −5 (additive-inverse idea: +3 cancels three of the −8, leaving −5). Target floor: (+5)+(−5) = 0. She ends on Floor 0. Method: combining button presses and additive inverse.
2 | A mine shaft runs from −180 m to +75 m. A worker begins at level −70 m and needs to reach level +75 m. What movement does the lift need to make? | Movement = target − start = (+75)−(−70). Subtracting a negative equals adding a positive: (+75)+(+70) = +145. The lift must move +145 m upward. Method: subtraction as movement needed (target floor minus starting floor).
3 | Use the token model to compute (−4)−(+5). Show your zero pairs. | Begin with 4 negative tokens. Need to remove 5 positive tokens — none present. Add 5 zero pairs (5 positive + 5 negative tokens) to the pool: pool is now 5 positive and 9 negative tokens. Remove the 5 positive tokens. Remaining: 9 negative tokens. (−4)−(+5) = −9. Method: token subtraction with zero pairs.
4 | Four temperatures recorded in Leh on one November day are −6°C, +2°C, −11°C, and −3°C. Write them in increasing order and find the difference between the highest and the lowest. | Increasing order: −11°C, −6°C, −3°C, +2°C. Difference = highest − lowest = (+2)−(−11) = (+2)+(+11) = +13. The range is 13°C. Method: integer comparison and ordering; subtraction of a negative.

materials: Blank paper or notebook for individual working

time_bands.activity: Teacher writes all four problems on the board and reads each aloud. No hints are given. Students copy the problems and begin individual work on all four.

Individual silent work. Every student writes full working for each problem — no bare answers. Teacher circulates without correcting, only prompting students who are stuck to return to the method: 'What does the target minus the start give you?' or 'How many zero pairs do you need to add?'
Groups of three compare answers. Any disagreement is settled by reconstructing the working step by step — the group must find exactly where the two routes diverged before moving on.

Whole-class presentations: one student per problem presents their solution at the board. After each presentation, the class names the chapter method the solution rested on. The teacher corrects only if the class cannot resolve an error themselves.

Closing: teacher states the chapter's one idea — every integer, however far from zero, has a precise place and can be added, subtracted, and compared using the same rules — and that is exactly why all four problems yielded.

items.prompt: In Bela's Building of Fun, the ground floor is Floor 0. The Video Games arcade is on Floor –2 and the Art Centre is on Floor +2. Which of the following correctly describes the relationship between these two floors?

options.label: A
options.text: Floor +2 is lower than Floor –2 because positive numbers are always smaller than negative numbers.

options.label: B
options.text: Floor –2 and Floor +2 are on the same level because they have the same absolute value.

options.label: C
options.text: Floor –2 is above Floor 0 because negative numbers are on the upper side of the building.

options.label: D
options.text: Floor –2 is below Floor 0, and Floor +2 is above Floor 0, so Floor –2 is lower than Floor +2.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Floor –2 is below Floor 0 and Floor +2 is above Floor 0, so Floor –2 is lower than Floor +2. In the building, floors below ground carry negative numbers and floors above carry positive numbers; a lower physical position means a smaller integer.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the building's vertical layout: negative floors are below ground (lower), positive floors are above (higher), so –2 < 0 < +2.

what_each_option_reveals.C: The student has reversed the sign convention, believing negative numbers correspond to upper floors.
what_each_option_reveals.B: The student confuses absolute value with value, thinking equal absolute values means equal integers.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student has inverted the positive/negative ordering entirely.

inclusivity.support: Allow the student to redraw the building diagram and physically point to the floor labelled –2 and the floor labelled +2 before deciding.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write the integers from –4 to +4 in order and explain what happens to the floor position as the integer increases by 1.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.1 p.245
exercise.description: Start from Floor +2 and press –3. Where do you reach? Write an expression.

items.prompt: A lift is on Floor –3. The lift attendant presses +5. Which floor does the lift reach, and what addition expression represents this journey?

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Floor +2. Starting at –3 and moving up 5 floors: –3 + 5 = +2. The correct expression is (–3)+(+5) = +2.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply Starting Floor + Movement = Target Floor: (–3)+(+5) = +2, counting 5 steps up from –3 on the vertical number line.

what_each_option_reveals.D: The student added the absolute values and kept the negative sign, ignoring the direction of the movement.
what_each_option_reveals.C: The student added 3 and 5 as positive values, ignoring the negative sign on the starting floor.
what_each_option_reveals.A: The student obtained the correct numerical answer but wrote the expression as subtraction of positives rather than addition of a negative and a positive.

inclusivity.support: Let the student trace the journey step by step on a drawn building: mark –3, then count upward five floors one at a time.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write a different starting floor and movement that still results in landing on Floor +2, and confirm using the rule.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.1 p.247
exercise.description: Compare six pairs of integers using < or > by referring to the Building of Fun: –2 vs +5, –5 vs +4, –5 vs –3, +6 vs –6, 0 vs –4, 0 vs +4.

items.prompt: Brahmagupta wrote one of his rules for addition as: 'The sum of two negative numbers is negative.' State this rule in your own words using the language of Bela's Building of Fun, and give a numerical example that matches the rule.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: If the lift is on a below-ground floor and you press a button that takes it further below ground, you end up on a floor with an even lower (more negative) number. For example, if you start on Floor –3 and press –4, you arrive at Floor –7, and –7 is negative. This matches Brahmagupta's rule that adding two negative numbers gives a negative result.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Translate 'negative number' as 'below-ground floor' and 'sum' as 'combined button press', then give a concrete floor example confirming the negative result.

inclusivity.support: Allow the student to look at the rules listed in section 10.5 of the textbook and identify which rule uses the word 'negative' twice before writing their own version.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to write the corresponding rule for subtracting a negative from a negative, give an example, and check whether the result is always negative or can be positive.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.5 p.268
exercise.description: Explain each of Brahmagupta's rules for addition and subtraction in terms of Bela's Building of Fun or the number line.

items.prompt: A hollow integer grid has eight border cells arranged around a 3×3 frame. The four border sums (top row, bottom row, left column, right column) must all equal the same value. Riya fills the border with the integers 1, –1, 2, –2, 3, –3, 0, 0 and claims the border sum must be 0. Is Riya necessarily correct? Explain your reasoning.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Riya is not necessarily correct. The border sum depends on which cells each integer is placed in, not merely on the set of integers used. The sum of all eight border values is 1+(–1)+2+(–2)+3+(–3)+0+0 = 0, but each individual row or column uses only some of those eight values (with corners shared between a row and a column). A specific arrangement might or might not produce equal border sums, and the border sum need not be 0. Riya would need to exhibit a valid arrangement with border sum 0 to justify her claim.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute the total of all eight border integers and reason about which subsets form each row or column, noting that the overall total alone does not fix the border sum.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student draw a blank 3×3 grid outline, label the eight border cells, and try placing the integers in two different ways to see whether the border sums change.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find one arrangement of those eight integers that gives border sum 0 and a different arrangement that does not give equal border sums, then explain what the difference is.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.4 p.263
exercise.description: Compute the four border sums (top row, bottom row, left column, right column) for the second hollow integer grid and identify the border sum.

items.prompt: In the amazing grid game, a student circles four numbers from a 4×4 integer grid by circling one number, striking its row and column, circling another unstruck number, striking its row and column, and repeating. She notices the sum of her four circled numbers is always the same no matter which numbers she picks. She tries a second grid and finds the same thing happens. Explain, without using algebra, why the sum might always stay the same regardless of the choices made.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Each time a number is circled, its entire row and column are eliminated, so the next circled number must come from a different row and a different column. This means every row and every column contributes exactly one circled number to the final total. Whatever specific numbers appear in the grid, the rule of one-per-row and one-per-column constrains which combinations are possible. When the grid is structured so that the numbers in each row and column are related by a fixed pattern (for example, an arithmetic progression), the total always works out the same because the 'extra' contributed by choosing a higher number in one row is exactly cancelled by being forced to choose a lower number somewhere else.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Reason that the one-per-row, one-per-column constraint means every valid selection picks exactly the same 'total contribution' from the grid's structure, so the sum is invariant.

inclusivity.support: Ask the student to try the game on the textbook grid twice with different starting choices, record the four circled numbers each time, and describe what is the same and what is different about the two selections.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to construct a small 3×3 version of such a grid with integer entries where the sum of any one-per-row, one-per-column selection is always –6, and verify with three different selections.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.4 p.265
exercise.description: In the amazing grid, try the circle-and-strike game afresh with different chosen numbers. Does the final sum change?

items.prompt: Consider these two integer expressions: (–8)–(–13) and 8+(–13). Without computing the final numerical answers, explain whether the two expressions are equal or unequal, and justify your reasoning using what you know about subtracting a negative number.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The two expressions are NOT equal. Subtracting a negative gives the same result as adding the corresponding positive, so (–8)–(–13) = (–8)+(+13) = +5. The expression 8+(–13) = 8–13 = –5. Since +5 ≠ –5, the two expressions are unequal. The confusion may arise because both involve the numbers 8 and 13, but the sign on 8 and the operation are different.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Convert (–8)–(–13) to (–8)+(+13) using the subtraction-of-a-negative rule, compute both, and compare.

inclusivity.support: Encourage the student to use the number line: draw an arrow for each expression starting from the given position and moving in the direction indicated, then compare the endpoints.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find a pair of integer expressions of the same structural form that ARE equal and explain why equality holds in that case but not in this one.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 10.4 p.265
exercise.description: Solve eight integer arithmetic expressions arranged in a 2×4 table: 8–13, (–8)–(13), (–13)–(–8), (–13)+(–8), 8+(–13), (–8)–(–13), (13)–8, 13–(–8).

items.prompt: Priya says: 'I can always find three different integers whose sum is any negative number I choose.' Is she right? Justify your answer with an argument, and give an example for the target sum –11.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Priya is right. For any negative target T, one approach is to write T = (T+1) + (–1) + 0, which uses three integers (T+1 is negative or zero since T is negative, –1 is negative, and 0 is an integer). Another approach: choose any two integers a and b; then the third integer needed is T–a–b, which is always a well-defined integer. For target –11 an example is: –5 + (–4) + (–2) = –11. One can verify: –5+(–4) = –9, and –9+(–2) = –11.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Fix any two integers freely; the third is determined as the target minus their sum, showing a valid triple always exists; verify the example by sequential addition.

inclusivity.support: Suggest starting with two negative integers that are easy to work with (such as –5 and –3), then figuring out what third integer is needed to reach –11.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find three integers that sum to –11 where all three integers are different and none is zero, then find a second such triple that uses at least one positive integer.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q2, section 10.4 p.265
exercise.description: Give three integers whose sum is –8.

items.prompt: A lift starts on Floor –6. It makes three movements in sequence: first it goes up 9 floors, then down 4 floors, then down 3 more floors. Write one addition expression for all three movements and find the floor the lift finally reaches. Verify your answer by checking that Starting Floor + Total Movement = Final Floor.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The three movements are +9, –4, and –3. Total movement = (+9)+(–4)+(–3) = +9–7 = +2. Starting floor + total movement = (–6)+(+2) = –4. So the lift reaches Floor –4. Verification: –6 + 2 = –4. ✓
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Sum the three movements to get total movement, then apply Starting Floor + Total Movement = Final Floor, and verify by reverse check.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student process one movement at a time: –6 then +9 gives +3; +3 then –4 gives –1; –1 then –3 gives –4.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to find a different sequence of three movements (with at least one negative) that also brings a lift from Floor –6 to Floor –4.

exercise.description: Complete ten subtraction expressions (a–j) as movement from Starting Floor to Target Floor: (+1)–(+4), 0–(+2), (+4)–(+1), 0–(–2), (+4)–(–3), (–4)–(–3), (–1)–(+2), (–2)–(–2), (–1)–(+1), (+3)–(–3).

items.prompt: A mine has levels measured in metres. Level 0 is the surface. A miner is at level –80 m. She needs to reach level +120 m (a tower above the surface). Write the subtraction expression that gives the total distance she must travel, compute the answer, and explain what the positive result means in this context.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The movement needed is Target – Starting = (+120)–(–80) = +120+(+80) = +200. The miner must travel +200 m upward. The positive result means the movement is upward (in the positive direction), and its magnitude is 200 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Apply Target Floor – Starting Floor = Movement, then convert subtraction of a negative to addition: (+120)–(–80) = +120+80 = +200.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student draw a vertical number line, mark –80 and +120, and count or compute the gap between them by first going from –80 to 0 (that is 80 steps up) then from 0 to +120 (another 120 steps up).
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student: if the miner then descends from +120 m back to –80 m, what is the movement for that journey, and how do the two movement values relate to each other?

exercise.description: Complete seven expressions using the mine/larger number context (a–g): (+40)+__=+200, (+40)+__=–200, (–50)+__=+200, (–50)+__=–200, (–200)–(–40), (+200)–(+40), (–200)–(+40). Verify using the mineshaft.

items.prompt: On an integer number line from –10 to +10, mark the positions –7, –3, +2, and +6. Then compute (+6)–(–7) using the number line by identifying the gap between the two marked points. Show your working.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: The gap from –7 to +6 on the number line is found by: (+6)–(–7) = +6+(+7) = +13. On the number line, moving from –7 rightward to 0 is 7 steps, then from 0 rightward to +6 is 6 more steps, giving a total of 13 steps. The answer is +13.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Use the number line to measure the rightward gap from –7 to +6, splitting at 0: 7 steps to 0 plus 6 steps to +6 equals 13; confirm with conversion (+6)–(–7) = +6+7 = +13.

inclusivity.support: Allow the student to count the tick marks between –7 and +6 one step at a time on the number line shown.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to use the same number line to compute (–3)–(+2) and explain why this result is negative while (+6)–(–7) is positive.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.1 p.253
exercise.description: Mark 3 positive and 3 negative numbers on a given number line (–10 to +10).

items.prompt: Use the token model to compute (+3)+(–7). Show the tokens you lay out, how many zero pairs you remove, and the tokens that remain. Write the final integer result.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Lay out 3 positive tokens and 7 negative tokens (10 tokens total). Remove 3 zero pairs (each pair = 1 positive + 1 negative). After removing the 3 zero pairs, 4 negative tokens remain. Therefore (+3)+(–7) = –4.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Lay out tokens for each integer, remove all zero pairs (one positive cancels one negative), and read the sign and count of the remaining tokens.

inclusivity.support: Allow the student to use actual paper squares labelled '+' and '–' and physically pair and set aside the zero pairs before counting what remains.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to verify the token-model result for (+3)+(–7) by also computing it on a number line (starting at +3 and moving 7 steps left) and confirm both methods give –4.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.2 p.257
exercise.description: Complete four additions using token diagrams: (+6)+(+4), (–3)+(–2), (+5)+(–7), (–2)+(+6).

items.prompt: Compute (–4)–(+3) using the token model. Explain how many zero pairs you needed to add (if any) and why, and state the final result.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Begin with 4 negative tokens. The instruction is to remove 3 positive tokens. There are no positive tokens in the pool, so add 3 zero pairs (3 positives + 3 negatives). The pool now has 3 positive tokens and 7 negative tokens. Remove the 3 positive tokens. The remaining pool has 7 negative tokens. Therefore (–4)–(+3) = –7. Three zero pairs were needed because there were no positive tokens to remove.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Start with 4 negatives; add 3 zero pairs to create the 3 positives needed; remove those 3 positives; count the 7 remaining negatives to get –7.

inclusivity.support: Remind the student that a zero pair (one positive + one negative together equal 0) can be added to the pool without changing the total value, then ask how many are needed so there are enough positive tokens to remove.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to verify the result by using the conversion rule: (–4)–(+3) = (–4)+(–3) = –7, and explain why both approaches give the same answer.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.2 p.258

items.prompt: Anika's bank account starts at ₹0. She receives a credit of ₹75, then makes a debit of ₹110, then receives a credit of ₹40. Write each transaction as a positive or negative integer, find the final balance, and state whether the account is in credit or in debit.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Transactions: +75, –110, +40. Final balance = 0 + 75 + (–110) + 40 = 75 – 110 + 40 = –35 + 40 = +5. Wait — recompute: 75 – 110 = –35; –35 + 40 = +5. The final balance is ₹+5, meaning the account is in credit by ₹5.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Represent each credit as a positive integer and each debit as a negative integer, then sum all transactions: 0 + 75 – 110 + 40 = +5.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student process one transaction at a time: start at 0, add +75 to get 75; add –110 to get –35; add +40 to get +5.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to change the debit amount to a value that would leave the account at exactly ₹0, and explain what that amount represents.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q1, section 10.3 p.260
exercise.description: Bank account: start at ₹0, add credits of ₹30, ₹40, ₹50 and debits of ₹40, ₹50, ₹60. What is the balance?

items.prompt: A geographical cross-section shows point P at –350 m (below sea level) and point Q at +210 m (above sea level). Write the subtraction expression for the difference in height from P to Q, compute the answer, and explain what a positive result means in this geographical context.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Difference = Q – P = (+210)–(–350) = +210+(+350) = +560 m. The result is positive, which means Q is higher than P. The vertical distance between the two points is 560 m.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Compute Q – P = (+210)–(–350) = +210+350 = +560, converting subtraction of a negative to addition; a positive result confirms Q is above P.

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student first find how far P is below sea level (350 m) and how far Q is above sea level (210 m), then add those two distances to find the total gap.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to compute P – Q instead, interpret the negative result, and explain how the two expressions P – Q and Q – P are related.

exercise.book_ref: Figure it Out Q4, section 10.3 p.261
exercise.description: What is the highest point above sea level on Earth and its height?

items.prompt: A lift starts at Floor –3. Over a day it makes the following movements: +7, –2, –5, +4, –1. Write a single addition expression for all five movements, compute the total movement, and find the floor where the lift ends the day. Then verify by computing: starting floor + total movement = ending floor.

teacher_guide.expected_answer: Total movement = (+7)+(–2)+(–5)+(+4)+(–1). Positives: 7+4 = 11. Negatives: (–2)+(–5)+(–1) = –8. Total movement = 11+(–8) = +3. Ending floor = Starting floor + Total movement = (–3)+(+3) = 0. Verification: –3 + 3 = 0. ✓ The lift ends the day on Floor 0.
teacher_guide.method_one_line: Separately sum all positive movements (11) and all negative movements (–8), combine to get total movement (+3), then add to starting floor (–3) to find the ending floor (0).

inclusivity.support: Suggest the student use the step-by-step method: apply each movement one at a time — –3, then +7 gives +4; +4 then –2 gives +2; +2 then –5 gives –3; –3 then +4 gives +1; +1 then –1 gives 0.
inclusivity.challenge: Ask the student to redesign the sequence of movements (keeping the same five values but changing their signs where desired) so the lift ends on Floor –5 instead of Floor 0, and verify the new ending floor.
